Imagism was an early twentieth-century modernist movement in poetry that demanded precise imagery, concision, and the abolition of nineteenth-century poetic conventions. Founded and theorized by Ezra Pound around 1912, it championed the direct presentation of images without rhetorical ornament or emotional commentary. Though the movement itself was short-lived, lasting roughly from 1912 to 1917, its principles profoundly shaped modernist and contemporary poetry.

Ezra Pound formulated the core doctrine: Direct treatment of the thing. No excess words. Every word must earn its place. The movement drew heavy influence from haiku and East Asian poetry, which prized economy and image over narrative or discursive meaning. Imagism rebelled against the late-Romantic tradition of elaborate description, didacticism, and sentimentality. Each poem was a single, crystallized moment of perception. The haiku form's structure—an intense image rendered in the fewest words—became the implicit template for imagist aesthetics.

Major imagist poets included Pound, Amy Lowell, and H.D., also known as Hilda Doolittle. Though their differing visions led to quick factional splits, imagism was never a large movement. But it redirected the entire energies of modernist verse. The principle of sharp, unadorned imagery became fundamental to twentieth-century poetry. The movement published chiefly in the periodical Poetry and collections like Des Imagistes in 1914, which circulated the aesthetic across the English-speaking literary world.

Amy Lowell took over leadership of the movement after Pound's departure and broader artistic interests pulled him toward other experiments like Vorticism. She expanded the imagist circle and extended its influence. The imagist principle—no ornament, no rhetoric, the image is the thing—outlasted the movement itself. It became a default assumption of modern and contemporary poetry. Modernism as a broader movement produced imagism as an avant-garde faction. Ezra Pound was the movement's chief theorist and strategist. Haiku, the Eastern form that influenced imagist principles of concision and image, provides the aesthetic model. Poetry as an art form was what imagism sought to revolutionize through purity and economy. T.S. Eliot was a poet shaped by imagist principles, though he developed in other directions. Stream of consciousness is another modernist technique emphasizing direct perception over conventional narration. Amy Lowell was a major imagist poet and publisher who promoted and eventually led the movement after Pound's departure.
